topic: AI Agent Deployment Infrastructure Guide 2026: Ampere.sh, E2B, Northflank, and Modal Compared

search_intent.primary: Help developers and technical buyers choose the right infrastructure layer for deploying AI agents in 2026.
secondary: Compare managed always-on agent hosting, secure code execution sandboxes, full-stack platform infrastructure, and Python/GPU serverless compute.
Clarify when each platform is appropriate instead of treating all agent infrastructure vendors as interchangeable sandbox providers.
Surface pricing, isolation, persistence, BYOC, GPU, and developer-experience tradeoffs.

executive_summary: The comparison should frame Ampere.sh, E2B, Northflank, and Modal as four different infrastructure categories rather than four direct clones. Ampere.sh is managed OpenClaw hosting for users who want an always-on agent without server setup. E2B is the narrowest and most agent-native secure code execution sandbox, with Firecracker isolation, SDK-first ergonomics, and clear session/concurrency limits. Northflank is the most complete production platform for teams that need BYOC, persistent services, databases, microVM isolation, and operational controls around agent workloads. Modal is best when the agent workload is tightly coupled to Python, GPU inference, batch jobs, or ML infrastructure, and its Sandboxes add untrusted-code execution to an already strong serverless compute platform.

positioning.best_for: Non-infrastructure teams that want to run OpenClaw agents continuously with messaging channels, hosting, credits, and managed setup bundled.
positioning.avoid_when: You need a generic code-execution sandbox API, GPU workloads, BYOC/VPC deployment, or arbitrary multi-tenant sandbox infrastructure.
positioning.key_takeaway: Ampere.sh should be evaluated as a managed agent product/runtime, not as a low-level sandbox provider.

positioning.best_for: Agent builders that need a purpose-built API for isolated code execution with fast onboarding, Python/JavaScript workflows, and Firecracker microVM isolation.
positioning.avoid_when: Workloads need unlimited runtime, broad platform services, built-in BYOC on lower tiers, or deep GPU-first ML deployment patterns.
positioning.key_takeaway: E2B is the default short-session sandbox choice when secure code execution is the center of the problem.

positioning.category: Full-stack AI workload platform with sandboxes
positioning.best_for: Production teams that need microVM-backed workloads, unlimited/persistent sessions, BYOC, services, jobs, databases, CI/CD, observability, and deployment governance in one control plane.
positioning.avoid_when: You only need a lightweight sandbox API for a prototype and do not want platform-level setup.
positioning.key_takeaway: Northflank is strongest when the agent is part of a larger production system, especially with compliance, data residency, or VPC constraints.

positioning.best_for: Python-heavy AI teams running inference, batch processing, agent code execution, notebooks, snapshots, and GPU workloads with per-second billing.
positioning.avoid_when: You need BYOC, a full application platform, or the simplest managed non-developer agent product.
positioning.key_takeaway: Modal is the best fit when agent infrastructure and ML compute infrastructure are the same operational problem.

stats.fact: Ampere.sh markets one-click OpenClaw deployment in 60 seconds with no server setup or maintenance.
Ampere.sh says users can bring their own API keys with zero markup or use Ampere credits, and can export data.

Ampere.sh comparison content lists OpenClaw via Ampere from $0/mo, with a free plan offering 5,000 credits, 2 vCPU, and 2GB RAM; paid tiers include Pro at $39/mo, Ultra at $79/mo, Unlimited at $299/mo, and Business custom pricing.
E2B states each sandbox is powered by Firecracker and can run up to 24 hours on Pro.
E2B pricing lists Hobby as free plus usage costs with a one-time $100 usage credit, 1-hour sandbox session length, and 20 concurrent sandboxes.
E2B pricing lists Pro at $150/mo plus usage costs with 24-hour session length, 100 concurrent sandboxes, and purchasable extra concurrency up to 1,100.
Northflank docs describe sandboxes as microVM-backed containers with VM-level isolation and container performance, booting in under 1 second.
Northflank docs describe BYOC sandbox deployment with microVM isolation enabled by default for workloads on microVM-enabled node pools.
Northflank's Developer Sandbox free plan allows 2 services, 2 jobs, 1 addon, and up to 1 BYOC cluster, but docs warn it should not be used for production applications.
Modal docs describe Sandboxes as secure containers for executing untrusted user or agent code.
Modal Sandbox resources are billed by the second based on whichever is higher: requested resources or actual usage.
Modal Sandboxes support snapshots for reducing startup latency, custom environments, debugging backups, large-scale experiments, and branching sandbox state.

article_angles: Do not ask which platform is best; ask what kind of agent infrastructure problem you have.
Ampere.sh vs E2B is product hosting vs code execution, not a direct API feature checklist.
E2B vs Northflank hinges on narrow sandbox API vs production platform control plane.
Northflank vs Modal hinges on full-stack deployment/BYOC vs Python-native serverless GPU workflows.
Modal vs E2B hinges on ML compute plus sandboxing vs sandboxing as the primary abstraction.
Session duration, persistence, snapshots, and state restoration are now first-class architecture criteria for agents.
Security posture should compare isolation model, network controls, resource limits, secrets handling, and auditability.
Pricing needs workload modeling: short bursty sessions, long-running idle agents, GPU-bound inference, and always-on managed agents produce different winners.

caveats: Several comparison articles are vendor-authored and should be treated as competitive positioning rather than neutral rankings.
Ampere.sh public pages are highly product-marketing oriented; hard infrastructure details are thinner than E2B, Northflank, and Modal documentation.
Pricing and limits can change quickly. Re-check provider pricing pages immediately before publication.

Northflank's strongest claims about unlimited sessions appear prominently in blog/market positioning; the article should cite official docs for microVM/BYOC facts and label long-session claims carefully if not backed by docs.
Modal Sandbox pricing should be sourced from Modal's official resource/pricing docs, with competitor pricing critiques used only as buyer-objection context.
